claims.text: Appropriately barium-doped, oxygen-controlled layered copper oxide perovskites will exhibit superconductivity.
Conductive CuO2 planes enable unconventional electron pairing in these materials.
Pristine, undoped La-based copper oxide perovskite is non-superconducting.
Controlled barium substitution and adjustment of oxygen stoichiometry can induce superconductivity in La-based copper oxide.
Precise control of synthesis temperature and oxygen environment stabilizes the perovskite lattice.
Precise control of synthesis temperature and oxygen environment enables optimal doping levels.
Barium substitution induces lattice distortions that facilitate the formation and ordering of CuO2 planes.
Variation in oxygen content facilitates the formation and ordering of CuO2 planes.
Barium doping and oxygen variation modify lattice vibrations and electronic correlations.
Modified lattice vibrations and electronic correlations enhance electron pairing.
The altered electronic environment promotes the onset of superconductivity.
The modified material will show a measurable drop in electrical resistance at its superconducting transition.
The modified material will have an elevated critical temperature relative to conventionally synthesized copper oxides.
Undoped La-based copper oxide remains insulating or non-superconducting under otherwise identical conditions.
Superconductivity occurs only within a narrow range of barium doping and oxygen content.
Outside the relevant barium-doping and oxygen-content ranges, the superconducting phase will not emerge.
Zero electrical resistance is an indicator of a superconducting transition.
A Meissner response in magnetic-susceptibility measurements is evidence of superconductivity.
